```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 100)
```

A transition tree is estimated from one sample of sequences. Every pathway it
reports, such as "after two active steps a learner stays active with
probability 0.79", is a statistic of that sample, and a different sample from
the same population would give a somewhat different count, a different
next-state distribution and, for pathways near the pruning threshold, a
different decision about whether the pathway exists at all. Variable-order
models are especially exposed to this. A context of depth three is observed
far less often than a context of depth one, and the deeper a pathway, the
fewer sequences carry it (Ron, Singer and Tishby, 1996; Bühlmann and Wyner,
1999). A pathway that a handful of sequences produce can look sharp and
distinctive in the fitted tree and still be an accident of who happened to be
sampled.

`bootstrap_pathways()` measures this sampling variability with a
non-parametric bootstrap at the level of the sequence. Each resample draws
whole sequences with replacement, so the dependence between the steps of a
sequence is kept, recounts every pathway of the fitted tree, and records its
statistics. The approach extends the edge-level bootstrap of transition
network analysis (Saqr et al., 2025) from single transitions to pathways of
variable depth. Two questions are asked of every pathway. **Stability** asks
whether the pathway's value reproduces: the share of resamples in which the
chosen statistic stays within a band around its observed value.
**Informativeness** asks whether the pathway reproducibly changes the
prediction: the share of resamples in which its likelihood-ratio statistic
against its shorter parent context exceeds the chi-square critical value, the
same test that `prune_tree(criterion = "G2")` applies once to the observed
data.

## Data

`trajectories` holds the engagement states of 138 learners over 15 time
steps.

- **Sequence:** one row per learner.
- **Time:** columns `1` to `15`, one per time step; trailing `NA`s mark the end of a
  shorter trajectory.
- **State:** `Active`, `Average` or `Disengaged`, the learner's engagement
  at that step.

```{r package}
library(transitiontrees)
dim(trajectories)
```

## The tree to resample

To fit the tree, we call `context_tree()` with `max_depth` for the longest
history considered and `min_count` for the minimum number of observations a
context needs to enter the tree. To keep only the contexts whose prediction
differs from their parent's, we call `prune_tree()`, which by default applies
a likelihood-ratio ($G^2$) test at $\alpha = 0.05$.

```{r fit}
tree <- context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 3L, min_count = 5L)
pruned <- prune_tree(tree)
pruned
```

The pruned tree keeps 18 of the 38 grown contexts: the root, three contexts
of depth one, eight of depth two and six of depth three. Two of the 138
learners have no recorded state, so the tree is fitted on 136 sequences and
1,870 observations.

## Running the bootstrap

To bootstrap the pathways, we call `bootstrap_pathways()` with `iter` for the
number of resamples and `seed` for a reproducible draw. By default stability
is measured on the pathway's count (`stat = "count"`) within the band
`consistency_range = c(0.5, 1.5)` times the observed value, a pathway is
`stable` when fewer than 5% of resamples fall outside the band
(`stability_threshold = 0.95`), and it is `informative` when its $G^2$
exceeds the critical value in at least 80% of resamples
(`informative_threshold = 0.80`). Two hundred resamples are used here so that
the guide builds quickly; a reported analysis should use the default of
1,000.

```{r boot}
boot <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200L, seed = 1L)
boot
```

The header states the rules. With three states the $G^2$ test against the
parent has two degrees of freedom, so its critical value is 5.99. Of the 18
pathways, 16 are stable, 12 are informative and all 12 informative pathways
are also stable. The table lists the trustworthy pathways first. The three
depth-one contexts and the depth-two pathways `Active -> Active`,
`Active -> Average`, `Average -> Active` and `Disengaged -> Average` clear
the critical value in every resample or nearly every one.

## The full summary table

To obtain one row per pathway with every bootstrap statistic, we call
`as.data.frame()` with `what = "summary"` (the default; `summary(boot)`
returns the same table). The table has 30 columns: the observed statistics,
the stability and informativeness measures, and the bootstrap mean, standard
deviation and percentile interval of the count, the probability of the most
likely next state, the divergence from the parent and $G^2$.

```{r summary-table}
reliability <- as.data.frame(boot, what = "summary")
dim(reliability)
names(reliability)
```

The definitions of the measures are:

- `p_stability`: the proportion of resamples, with a +1 correction, in which
  the statistic falls outside the band; `stable` is `TRUE` when it is below
  `1 - stability_threshold`. With 200 resamples its smallest possible value
  is 1/201 = 0.005.
- `stability_rate`: the uncorrected proportion of resamples inside the band.
  A pathway that is absent from a resample has a count of zero there and
  falls outside the band.
- `informative_rate`: the proportion of resamples in which
  $G^2 = 2 \sum_j n_j \log\{n_j / (n\, p_j^{\text{parent}})\}$, with $n_j$
  the counts of the next states after the pathway and $p^{\text{parent}}$ the
  empirical distribution of its parent context, exceeds the critical value
  $\chi^2_{0.95,\,k-1}$.
- `flip_consistency`: the proportion of resamples that reproduce whether the
  pathway's most likely next state differs from its parent's.
- `divergence`: the Kullback-Leibler divergence, in bits, of the pathway's
  next-state distribution from its parent's.

All statistics are computed from raw counts: no smoothing and no `min_count`
filter are applied inside the resampling loop.

## Confidence intervals for pathway statistics

To report each pathway's observed $G^2$ with its 95% bootstrap interval, we
call `subset()` on the summary table with `select` for the columns.

```{r g2-ci}
subset(reliability, select = c(pathway, depth, count, G2, ci_G2_lo,
                               ci_G2_hi, informative_rate))
```

The interval for `Active` runs from 253 to 400, far above the critical value
of 5.99. The pathways that the pruning test kept with the least margin are
the deep ones. `Active -> Average -> Average` has an observed $G^2$ of 11.3
with an interval from 2.9 to 26.8; it clears the critical value in 87.5% of
resamples and so is informative, though with far less margin than the
depth-one pathways. The depth-three pathways `Active -> Average -> Disengaged`,
`Disengaged -> Average -> Active` and `Disengaged -> Active -> Average`, with
10 to 17 observations each, have intervals whose lower bounds lie near 1 and
clear the critical value in 58% to 70% of resamples: the pruning test kept
them on the observed sample, but they would be dropped in a large share of
resamples.

The interval on the probability of the most likely next state is the
statement a reader of a pathway usually needs.

```{r prob-ci}
subset(reliability, depth == 2,
       select = c(pathway, count, likely_next, next_probability,
                  ci_next_probability_lo, ci_next_probability_hi))
```

After two active steps the probability of a third is 0.79, with a 95%
interval from 0.73 to 0.83.

## The four kinds of pathway

Stability and informativeness answer different questions, and a pathway is
worth interpreting when it passes both. The two flags divide the pathways
into four groups: stable and informative (a reproducible and distinctive
pathway), stable only (a reproducible pathway whose prediction is close to its
parent's), informative only (a distinctive pathway carried by an unstable
subset of sequences), and neither. To list the pathways that are stable but
not informative, we call `subset()` with a condition on the two flags.

```{r stable-only}
subset(reliability, stable & !informative,
       select = c(pathway, count, stability_rate, informative_rate, G2))
```

The root, `(start)`, has no parent, so it has no $G^2$ and is never
informative. `Average -> Average`, with 419 observations, is the clearest case: its count
reproduces in every resample, but its prediction is close enough to that of
`Average` that its $G^2$ exceeds the critical value in 76% of resamples.
Pruning kept it on the observed sample; the bootstrap shows that
the extra step of history it adds is not reproducibly informative.

To list the pathways that fail the stability criterion, we use the same call
with `!stable`.

```{r unstable}
subset(reliability, !stable,
       select = c(pathway, count, ci_count_lo, ci_count_hi, stability_rate))
```

Both unstable pathways are depth-three contexts with 10 and 12 observations,
and both stay inside the band in 94% of resamples, short of the 95%
required. Their 95% count intervals span more than a factor of three, which is
the signature of a pathway that a few learners carry.

## The forest plot

To see $G^2$ and its interval for every pathway at once, we call `plot()` on
the bootstrap result. Pathways are ordered with the stable and informative
ones first; the dashed line is the critical value. By default only pathways
whose `stability_rate` reaches the stability threshold are drawn; `top` caps
the number of rows.

```{r forest, fig.height = 5}
plot(boot)
```

A pathway whose interval lies entirely to the right of the dashed line is
reproducibly informative. Intervals that cross the line belong to pathways
whose informativeness depends on the sample.

## Resample distributions

An interval summarizes a distribution, and a skewed or bimodal distribution
can hide behind a symmetric-looking interval. To draw the full resample
distribution of a statistic for the leading pathways, we call
`plot_pathway_resamples()` with `stat` for the statistic and `top` for the
number of pathways.

```{r resamples-g2, fig.height = 4.2}
plot_pathway_resamples(boot, stat = "G2", top = 6L)
```

To draw chosen pathways, we pass their names to `pathways`.

```{r resamples-chosen, fig.height = 3.2}
plot_pathway_resamples(boot, stat = "next_probability",
                       pathways = c("Active -> Active",
                                    "Average -> Average",
                                    "Active -> Average -> Average"))
```

The 95% interval of the probability of the most likely next state is 0.73
to 0.83 for `Active -> Active` and 0.44 to 0.69 for
`Active -> Average -> Average`, which has about a fifth of the observations.

To obtain the resample values themselves, one row per resample and pathway,
we call `as.data.frame()` with `what = "resamples"` and `stat` for the
statistic. A pathway absent from a resample has `NA` for statistics that
need at least one observation.

```{r resamples-table}
resamples <- as.data.frame(boot, what = "resamples", stat = "G2")
head(subset(resamples, pathway == "Average -> Average"))
dim(resamples)
```

The table has 200 resamples times 18 pathways, 3,600 rows. It is the input
for any summary of the resample distribution that the package does not
compute itself.

## Sensitivity to the bootstrap settings

The band, the thresholds and the seed are analytic choices, and a reported
reliability result should survive a reasonable change in each. To measure
stability on the probability of the most likely next state instead of the
count, with a narrower band, we call `bootstrap_pathways()` with `stat` and
`consistency_range`.

```{r sensitivity-stat}
boot_prob <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200L, seed = 1L,
                                stat = "next_probability",
                                consistency_range = c(0.75, 1.25))
print(boot_prob, n = 3L)
```

To check the result against a different random draw, we change `seed`.

```{r sensitivity-seed}
boot_seed <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200L, seed = 2L)
print(boot_seed, n = 3L)
```

To demand that a pathway clear the critical value in 95% of resamples rather
than 80%, we set `informative_threshold`.

```{r sensitivity-threshold}
boot_strict <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200L, seed = 1L,
                                  informative_threshold = 0.95)
print(boot_strict, n = 3L)
```

The first run found 16 stable and 12 informative pathways. Measuring
stability on the next-state probability with the narrower band leaves 15
stable pathways and 11 that are both: `Active -> Disengaged` (23
observations) loses its stability, and `Active -> Average -> Disengaged`
replaces `Disengaged -> Average -> Active` among the unstable ones. A second
seed reproduces the same 16 stable and 12 informative pathways. The stricter
informativeness threshold of 0.95 keeps 9 of the 12. A conclusion about a
specific pathway should be reported only if it holds under all of these
settings.

## Resampling the unpruned tree

Pruning and the bootstrap answer related questions, and the bootstrap can be
run on the unpruned tree to see which of the grown contexts it would support.

```{r unpruned}
boot_full <- bootstrap_pathways(tree, iter = 200L, seed = 1L)
print(boot_full, n = 5L)
```

Of the 38 grown contexts, 30 are stable and 12 are reproducibly
informative, and the 12 are the same pathways that were informative in the
pruned tree. The single $G^2$ test of `prune_tree()` kept 17 contexts below
the root; the bootstrap supports 12 of them and adds what the single test
cannot: the share of resamples in which each decision would have been made.

## Summary

| Question | Call |
|---|---|
| Does each pathway reproduce and change the prediction? | `bootstrap_pathways(tree, iter = 1000L, seed = 1L)` |
| The full table of bootstrap statistics | `as.data.frame(boot, what = "summary")` or `summary(boot)` |
| Confidence intervals for one statistic | `subset(as.data.frame(boot), select = c(pathway, ci_G2_lo, ci_G2_hi))` |
| Pathways in one reliability group | `subset(as.data.frame(boot), stable & !informative)` |
| Every resample value | `as.data.frame(boot, what = "resamples", stat = "G2")` |
| $G^2$ intervals for all pathways | `plot(boot)` |
| The resample distribution of a statistic | `plot_pathway_resamples(boot, stat = "G2")` |

Smoothing and the pruning test are covered in
[Smoothing and pruning](smoothing-and-pruning.html), and the comparison of
pathways between groups in
[Comparing groups](comparing-groups.html).
